ratings.rationale: Association corruption can fabricate, merge or lose tracks through incorrect measurement grouping. It is distinct from measurement tampering. No mechanism is published; host-level exploitation requires substantial access. Neither downstream integrity check necessarily validates association correctness.
ratings.issue: The record conflates track fabrication and denial; distinguish association integrity from subsequent solver and tracker failures.

ratings.rationale: Changing detection logic is distinct from changing thresholds: it alters predicate semantics and can suppress or invent verdicts. It enables downstream deception or denial rather than necessarily changing a position itself. No supporting mechanism is cited.
ratings.issue: Monitor and cross-check are separate assets; identify which logic is modified and distinguish this from T3.06.

ratings.rationale: Corrupted ephemerides or clock-state inputs bias localisation independently of the original observable timing source. The effect is solver-input tampering. Strong-pass detection follows W2; weak-pass stealth follows W3. No published mechanism is cited.
ratings.issue: The asserted equivalence to clock bias is conditional; ephemeris and clock-state corruption have different residual and detection characteristics.

ratings.rationale: Post-association modification of solver inputs is a distinct data-plane compromise, although it overlaps corrupted database inputs. Authentication of transport does not protect internal processing. Position displacement is possible; detection depends on the resulting solution and pass conditions.
ratings.issue: Specify whether measurements or metadata are changed; the boundary between association output and solver input is insufficiently defined.

ratings.rationale: Resource exhaustion prevents timely surveillance solutions and is a genuine availability threat. The cited spacecraft vulnerability presentation is not direct evidence of this specific processing mechanism. Analogue evidence is insufficient to establish demonstrated LEO-MLAT exploitability.
ratings.issue: Source 65 is a non-peer-reviewed talk and does not establish solver-specific exhaustion; affected-user extent depends on workload isolation.

ratings.rationale: Threshold relaxation changes configuration rather than detection logic. It expands the weak-pass stealth window and is an enabler of subsequent displacement. Strong-pass protection remains governed by W2. No published malicious threshold-relaxation mechanism is cited.
ratings.issue: The claim that all routes are affected simultaneously requires shared configuration and successful propagation.

ratings.rationale: Consistent false surveillance positions defeat the intended independence of the cross-check. Multi-emitter multilateration spoofing has published experimental support, but transfer to this LEO architecture is analogue-only. W2 and W3 determine detection differences.
ratings.issue: The cited terrestrial multilateration results do not establish simultaneous consistency across LEO geometry and the broadcast-position comparison.

ratings.rationale: Creating a false discrepancy can produce an incorrect integrity verdict against a genuine aircraft. This is distinct from consistent false-position acceptance. The cited track-verification and multilateration work is relevant but analogue to the specified architecture.
ratings.issue: Identify which independent position is perturbed; the record does not establish that a suspect annotation necessarily removes or discredits the target.

ratings.rationale: Output tampering occurs after the stated L3 integrity predicates, potentially altering both surveillance content and integrity annotations. It is a distinct downstream integrity failure. No mechanism-specific published evidence is supplied.
ratings.issue: The attack may be realised at the L4 delivery interface rather than L3; downstream ATM validation and feed protections are omitted.

ratings.rationale: Unauthorised track and report access is a standalone confidentiality threat, with no stated downstream enabling role. Disclosure is the defined damage class. No cited mechanism supports a higher evidence rating.
ratings.issue: A3.6 is an encoder and gateway, not the track database; include A3.3 and distinguish stored records from delivered traffic.

ratings.rationale: Suppressing or altering audit records undermines attribution and investigation, fitting repudiation. It does not independently change surveillance output. The cited general spacecraft-security presentation is only indirect support for log manipulation.
ratings.issue: Audit logs are not explicitly registered as an asset; distinguish audit suppression from alteration of operational track records.

ratings.rationale: Compromise of the shared processing host provides broad control over surveillance functions and can defeat module-level trust assumptions. It is primarily privilege escalation, with integrity, availability and confidentiality consequences. Source 65 is indirect, non-peer-reviewed evidence.
ratings.issue: The claim of control over every module assumes common host privileges and no effective isolation; the cited source does not demonstrate this CPS architecture.

missing_threats.title: Unauthorised ephemeris product substitution
missing_threats.why: Compromise of orbit determination or its product distribution is distinct from corruption of the central working database.

missing_threats.title: Configuration provenance and rollback failure
missing_threats.why: Malicious or unauthorised firmware and configuration rollback can undermine lower-layer protections.

missing_threats.title: Credential and key compromise
missing_threats.why: Credential theft enables authorised-looking access to command, link and management functions.

missing_threats.title: ATM feed substitution or replay
missing_threats.why: Delivery and consumption introduce independent freshness, authenticity and integrity risks.

missing_threats.title: Measurement association ambiguity
missing_threats.why: Legitimate simultaneous transmissions and ambiguous receptions can cause incorrect associations without software compromise.

rubric_ambiguities: The rubric does not specify whether an enabler receives discoverability scores based on its own detection or its enabled threat.
STRONG and WEAK predicates are defined for single-satellite timing bias, not every L3 corruption mechanism.
Affected users can mean simultaneous aircraft, geographically exposed users or total service population.
Evidence levels do not clearly distinguish general platform vulnerability demonstrations from evidence of the specific attack mechanism.
The tier-to-exploitability mapping does not explain how authorised insiders with different access levels should be scored.
batch_comments.overall: The batch covers important L3 integrity, availability, confidentiality and platform threats. Several records need clearer asset boundaries and separation of configuration tampering, logic tampering and data tampering. Published support is generally weak or analogue-only. The strongest concern is broad compromise of shared processing and downstream report integrity; the timing-specific detection assumptions should not automatically be generalized to every threat.
